title: Iran Rebuilds Military Infrastructure Far Faster Than Israel Expected
excerpt: Satellite imagery and intelligence assessments show Tehran has reconstructed missile bases, bridges, and production facilities within weeks of strikes, restoring at least half its pre-war missile stockpile.
body:
• Satellite imagery reveals Iran has reconstructed damaged missile bases, bridges, and production facilities within weeks of Israeli and U.S. strikes
  • Israeli intelligence estimates Tehran has restored at least half its pre-war stockpile of roughly 2,700 missiles
  • Iran has restarted production of ballistic missiles, drones, and air defense systems using surviving components and older manufacturing methods
  • The faster-than-expected rebuild has prompted Israeli officials to question their targeting strategy's long-term effectiveness

Iran has rapidly reconstructed critical military infrastructure destroyed during its wars with Israel and the United States, with satellite imagery and intelligence assessments showing a pace of recovery that has alarmed Israeli defense planners and raised questions about the durability of air campaigns against Tehran's military apparatus.

Rebuilding at Speed

Commercial satellite imagery from Planet Labs and Airbus, reviewed by the Wall Street Journal, shows substantial reconstruction across multiple Iranian provinces. Near Kangavar in western Iran, two tunnel entrances to an underground missile base that had been sealed by precision airstrikes were reopened within weeks, with freshly paved access roads visible in subsequent images.

https://x.com/GanjiAkbar/status/2088597332203884747

The recovery extends to strategic transit infrastructure. An Israeli military official told the Journal that Iranian repair crews restored a bridge within days of it being struck with three heavy bombs — a timeline that prompted Jerusalem to reassess its battle damage assessments across the Iranian theater.

At the port of Bandar Anzali on the Caspian Sea, imagery from early July showed partial reconstruction of a shipyard linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). Israel had struck dozens of targets there in March, including warships, a command center, and a shipyard used to maintain vessels along a Russia-Iran supply line.

"They filled up their stocks again. They have very impressive industrialization and reconstruction capabilities."

— Ran Kochav, Former Commander, Israeli Air and Missile Defense Forces

Missile Production Restarts

Israeli intelligence assessments, reported by the news outlet Mako, confirm that Iran has resumed limited manufacturing of ballistic missiles, launch platforms, and anti-aircraft systems using surviving components and production lines that either escaped destruction or have already been restored. Tehran has also recovered missiles and launchers from underground tunnel systems damaged during the conflict.

Before the June 2025 war, Israeli intelligence estimated Iran held roughly 2,700 missiles. Officials now believe the Islamic Republic has restored at least half that stockpile and is working to expand it beyond pre-war levels, according to the American Israelite. Iranian lawmakers and commanders have promoted a policy of "ballistic missiles without limits," with senior officers stating Tehran will extend its missile range "to any necessary extent."

Factories are reportedly operating around the clock, though Iran has been forced to rely on older manufacturing methods after Israel destroyed planetary mixers — specialized machines essential for producing solid rocket fuel used in medium- and long-range missiles. Experts say acquiring new mixers, likely from China, remains a priority for Tehran.

A Pattern of Underestimation

The rapid recovery echoes a pattern that emerged after the 12-day Israel-Iran war in June 2025. During that conflict, Israel's Operation Rising Lion killed several senior Iranian commanders, including the chief of staff of the armed forces and the head of the IRGC. The U.S. struck three Iranian nuclear sites. Despite Iran firing hundreds of missiles and more than 1,000 attack drones during the conflict, initial assessments suggested its military was severely degraded.

Those assessments proved premature. By February 2026, renewed hostilities had erupted, with Iran launching fresh attacks on Israel and Gulf states.

"They underestimated the Iranian ability to regroup after very successfully targeting the top leadership of the Iranian military."

— Trita Parsi, Vice President, Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft

Implications for the Region

The reconstruction has broader implications for the Middle East. Iran's cyberattacks against Israel have surged alongside its conventional rebuilding — from roughly 1,600 incidents in June 2025 to some 4,800 in June 2026, according to Yossi Karadi, director general of Israel's National Cyber Directorate. Defense analysts warn that if Iran perceives a threat to regime survival, its calculus on retaliation could shift dramatically, potentially targeting U.S. bases, oil infrastructure, and the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly a fifth of the world's oil transits.

What's Next

Israeli officials now face a strategic dilemma: repeated air campaigns have failed to permanently degrade Iran's military-industrial capacity. With diplomatic negotiations ongoing alongside the conflict, Tehran appears to be exploiting any pauses to accelerate reconstruction. The question for Israeli and American planners is whether sustained pressure can outpace Iran's ability to rebuild — or whether a fundamentally different approach is needed.
